---
title: "Insight from Psychedelic Research"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-31"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

While the plasticity-enhancing treatments discussed in this paper share a common foundation in promoting neuroplasticity, they exhibit distinct clinical profiles and temporal dynamics. If their mechanisms of action were merely duplicative, their combination would be redundant and offer little added benefit. Yet, clinical practice frequently employs and finds value in combination treatments, such as maintenance pharmacotherapy following ECT, psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy, or the concurrent use of rTMS with medication.

This suggests that while these treatments operate under shared principles, they may have distinct roles in the treatment process. Currently, the field lacks a unifying framework to guide their integration, often relying on sequential or trial-and-error approaches. Developing rational combination strategies that account for individual patient's symptom characteristics and treatment history requires a clearer mapping of where each intervention is uniquely positioned along the axis of treatment process.

In this context, psychedelic research provides a valuable insight. Substances like psilocybin, LSD, and DMT transiently dismantle canonical functional networks and facilitate global re-integration [@Tagliazucchi2018]. This phenomenon has been conceptualized as an "entropic brain state," where the brain transitions into a more flexible regime near "criticality" [@CarhartHarris2014; @CarhartHarris2019]. This disruption is considered therapeutic, as it enables the brain to escape from pathological "stuck loops." Recent fMRI studies have confirmed that this acute desynchronization allows the system to access a broader repertoire of potential brain states, effectively liberating it from the rigid dynamics associated with psychopathology [@Siegel2024].

Another important insight is that these substances can reopen critical periods for neuroplastic learning [@Hensch2004; @Patton2019]. A critical period is an early developmental window during which the nervous system is exceptionally sensitive to environmental stimuli, allowing for the acquisition of essential knowledge for survival. Animal studies have demonstrated that the administration of psychedelics to adult mice can re-engage critical periods, particularly in the context of social reward learning [@Nardou2023]. Re-entering a critical period signifies a substantial elevation in neuroplastic potential, facilitating rapid and sustained modifications in structural and functional connectivity. Reflecting this capacity, psychedelics are often termed "psychoplastogens" [@Vargas2021]. At the cellular level, these agents promote synaptogenesis in the cortex and hippocampus within hours, either by stimulating BDNF production or by binding directly to the TrkB receptor [@Moliner2023; @Shafiee2024].

Clinicians practicing psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy view this critical period as a "window of opportunity" for therapeutic change, emphasizing that intensive psychotherapeutic interventions must be provided during this time [@CarhartHarris2018; @Lepow2021; @Lepow2023; @Caulfield2025]. This clinical expertise underscores that the critical period reopened by psychedelics serves as a prime opportunity for fundamental change in any direction.

These features of psychedelics map naturally onto an attractor model of psychopathology. Acute $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$-mediated perturbation transiently reduces within- and between-network integrity, leading to a temporary “flattening” of the attractor landscape and enhanced transitions among metastable states [@Roseman2014; @Madsen2021; @Singleton2022]. Following this disruption, a time-limited window of heightened neuroplasticity opens, during which activity-dependent synaptic remodeling is facilitated via BDNF–TrkB-linked pathways. Clinically, psychedelic-assisted interventions show transdiagnostic efficacy, yet these benefits appear to be time-limited; without structured psychotherapy and positive environmental stimuli, clinical gains may attenuate as the system relaxes back toward pre-existing maladaptive attractors [@CarhartHarris2018a; @Goodwin2022]. In terms of dynamical systems theory, this window corresponds to a sufficiently flattened and malleable landscape that permits the reconstruction of attractor geometry as new basins are formed and constraining conditions are altered. Subsequent treatment can be visualized as a process of delicate sculpting, reinforcing the dynamic resilience of healthy basins and preventing the system from becoming trapped in pathological states.
